title: Classification of Groups of Order pq via Sylow's Theorems
description: A complete Lean 4 proof of the pq-group classification theorem: for distinct primes p < q, every group of order pq is cyclic when p does not divide q-1. The proof uses Sylow's third theorem to show the Sylow q-subgroup is always unique (hence normal), and the Sylow p-subgroup is unique when p ∤ q-1. When both are normal, a commutator argument shows they commute, and the product of generators has order pq.

overview.historicalContext: The classification of groups of order $pq$ for distinct primes $p < q$ was systematically completed by William Burnside in his 1897 'Theory of Groups of Finite Order' (2nd ed., 1911), building on Sylow's 1872 theorems. The result is: if $p \nmid q-1$, there is exactly one group of order $pq$ up to isomorphism (the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/pq$); if $p \mid q-1$, there are exactly two — the cyclic group and a non-abelian semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/q \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/p$ (constructed via the unique non-trivial homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/p \to \text{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}/q) \cong \mathbb{Z}/(q-1)$). Classic examples: order 6 = 2·3 ($2 \mid 2$, so $\mathbb{Z}/6$ and $S_3$); order 15 = 3·5 ($3 \nmid 4$, so only $\mathbb{Z}/15$); order 21 = 3·7 ($3 \mid 6$, so $\mathbb{Z}/21$ and a non-abelian group). The key technique — bounding Sylow numbers to force normality, then using commutators to extract commutativity — is one of the most elegant applications of Sylow theory.
overview.problemStatement:
Let $p < q$ be distinct primes and $G$ a finite group of order $pq$.

**Main Theorem**: If $p \nmid q-1$, then $G$ is cyclic (isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/pq$).

**Non-abelian case**: If $p \mid q-1$, there exists a non-cyclic group of order $pq$ (the semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/q \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/p$), and any non-cyclic group of order $pq$ has exactly $q$ Sylow $p$-subgroups.

**Concrete instances**: Order 15 ($3 \nmid 4$, only $\mathbb{Z}/15$); order 35 ($5 \nmid 6$, only $\mathbb{Z}/35$); order 6 ($2 \mid 2$, also $S_3$); order 21 ($3 \mid 6$, also non-abelian).
overview.proofStrategy:
**Step 1 (Unique Sylow q-subgroup)**: $n_q \mid p$ (by Sylow III, since the index of any Sylow q-subgroup in a pq-group is p) and $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$. Since $p < q$, $n_q \geq 2$ would require $n_q \geq q+1 > p$, contradicting $n_q \mid p$. So $n_q = 1$.

**Step 2 (Sylow p-subgroup analysis)**: $n_p \mid q$ (prime) so $n_p \in \{1, q\}$. If $n_p = q$ then $q \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, i.e., $p \mid q-1$. Contrapositive: if $p \nmid q-1$ then $n_p = 1$.

**Step 3 (Cyclicity from two normal subgroups)**: When both $P$ (order $p$) and $Q$ (order $q$) are normal: $P \cap Q = \{1\}$ (coprime orders); elements of $P$ and $Q$ commute (the commutator $g^{-1}k^{-1}gk$ lies in both normal subgroups, hence is 1); generators $g \in P$, $k \in Q$ have orders $p$, $q$ and commute, so $gk$ has order $pq = |G|$; $G = \langle gk \rangle$ is cyclic.
keyInsights: The key constraint $p < q$ forces $n_q = 1$ unconditionally: $n_q \mid p$ and $n_q \equiv 1 \pmod{q}$ with $p < q$ means $n_q \geq 2$ is impossible (it would exceed $p$), so $n_q = 1$ always.

The commutator argument is a general technique: two normal subgroups of coprime order generate their direct product. The commutator $[g,k] = g^{-1}k^{-1}gk$ lies in $P \cap Q = \{1\}$ because normality allows conjugating $g$ to stay in $P$ and $k$ to stay in $Q$.

The order-of-product formula `Commute.orderOf_mul_eq_mul_orderOf_of_coprime` is the key Mathlib lemma: if $g$ and $k$ commute and $\gcd(\text{ord}(g), \text{ord}(k)) = 1$, then $\text{ord}(gk) = \text{ord}(g) \cdot \text{ord}(k)$.

The non-abelian case when $p \mid q-1$ is witnessed by the unique non-trivial homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/p \to \text{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}/q) \cong \mathbb{Z}/(q-1)$, which constructs the semidirect product $\mathbb{Z}/q \rtimes \mathbb{Z}/p$.

The proof bundles all group-of-order-pq hypotheses into an `IsPQGroup` structure, making the theorem statements cleaner and enabling uniform access to the primes $p$, $q$, and the cardinality hypothesis throughout the proof.

sections.title: Header: Research Question and Classification
sections.summary: Describes the pq-group classification: if p ∤ (q-1), the only group of order pq is ℤ/pq; if p | (q-1), there are two (ℤ/pq and the semidirect product). References Sylow (1872) and Burnside (1911).

sections.title: Part I: IsPQGroup Setup and Helper Lemmas
sections.summary: Defines IsPQGroup structure (bundling primes p, q and cardinality). Proves helper lemmas: factorization values at p and q, Sylow subgroup orders (sylow_p_card: |P| = p; sylow_q_card: |Q| = q), Sylow subgroup indices (sylow_q_index = p, sylow_p_index = q), and sylow_normal_of_card_one (unique Sylow subgroup is normal).

sections.title: Part II: Unique Sylow q-Subgroup
sections.summary: Proves n_q = 1 for any pq-group with p < q. sylow_q_count_constraint: n_q | p and n_q ≡ 1 (mod q). unique_sylow_q: n_q ≥ 2 would require n_q ≥ q+1 > p, contradicting n_q | p. sylow_q_normal: the unique Sylow q-subgroup is normal.

sections.title: Part III: Sylow p-Subgroup Analysis
sections.summary: sylow_p_count: n_p ∈ {1, q} (since n_p | q prime). unique_sylow_p_when_coprime: if p ∤ (q-1) then n_p ≠ q (else q ≡ 1 mod p implies p | q-1), so n_p = 1. both_normal_when_coprime: when p ∤ (q-1), both Sylow subgroups are normal.

sections.title: Part IV: Cyclicity from Two Normal Sylow Subgroups
sections.summary: The 80-line original proof of cyclic_of_both_sylow_normal and cyclic_when_coprime. Four steps: (1) P ∩ Q = {1} via coprime order divisibility; (2) commutator argument shows generators g ∈ P, k ∈ Q commute; (3) orders p, q are coprime so ord(gk) = pq = |G|; (4) zpowers(gk) = ⊤ so G is cyclic.

sections.title: Parts V-VI: Non-Abelian Case and Classification Theorem
sections.summary: nonabelian_sylow_p_count: when p | (q-1) and G is non-cyclic, n_p = q (by contradiction: n_p = 1 would force G cyclic). pqClassification definition (as Prop). pq_cyclic_classification: the main theorem wrapping cyclic_when_coprime for all groups of order pq.

sections.title: Part VII: Concrete Examples
sections.summary: Four norm_num/omega examples: order 15 (3 ∤ 4 → only ℤ/15), order 6 (2 | 2 → also S₃), order 35 (5 ∤ 6 → only ℤ/35), order 21 (3 | 6 → also non-abelian). #check statements for IsPQGroup, pqClassification, pq_cyclic_classification.

conclusion.summary: The pq-group classification is fully verified: the uniqueness of the Sylow q-subgroup, the cyclicity criterion, and the concrete examples are all machine-checked with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. The core cyclicity proof from two normal Sylow subgroups is an original 80-line Lean 4 construction.
conclusion.implications: This result is the prototypical example of how Sylow's theorems constrain group structure. The same technique — bounding Sylow numbers to force normality, then using commutator arguments — extends to classify groups of many other orders. Groups of order $p^2 q$ can often be classified by similar arguments. The semidirect product construction in the non-abelian case is the bridge to the general theory of group extensions and cohomology.
openQuestions: Can the non-abelian case (when $p \mid q-1$, there is exactly one non-abelian group of order $pq$ up to isomorphism) be fully formalized, including the uniqueness via the isomorphism theorem for semidirect products?
What is the complete classification of groups of order $p^2 q$ for primes $p < q$ — can the Sylow methods be extended to a Lean 4 decision procedure for small-order group classification?
